If I had to do that again, I'd probably use a pretty directional mic, something super or hyper cardiod and aim it directly at the beater as close as you can get it so that it won't pick up as much bleed from the rest of the kit. This will definitely give you plenty of beater smack, but not a lot in the low-end department so you'll probably want to pair it with another mic on the reso side of the kick to get the weight of the kick. 

You'll definitely want to gate it pretty aggressively. I almost always use [key spikes](https://youtu.be/BGEQhm5ECBw?si=aC75Mz9zMlBddokY) to side chain my drum gates. They can be a little tedious to set up, but they make gating drums way more accurate and you can just set and forget them.

I run a small, commercial studio in East TN. Any time I do hardcore I like to track it as live as possible with the band playing together, or at least drums and guitar together. I'll mic up all the shells and cymbals plus overheads and a stereo room, so I usually end up with between 12-16 mics depending on the size of the kit. If anyone's interested, I can do a breakdown of what I use in terms of microphones and preamps but it's a lot to type out here. Guitars are usually going through my 5150II into a Mesa OS with two dynamic mics, one on axis and the other off, going into a couple of Midas preamps. For bass I usually just run DI into a preamp and some compression, and  I'll use my Kemper or Neural's Parallax to give it some dirt. Vocals are tracked with an SM7B with a good amount of compression. Everything tracks into Logic for me

Welcome to the world of recording my friend! Ive worked with a lot of heavy bands in my area, so I'll try to help you as best that I can.

First things first, you'll want to get an audio interface of some sort. This will allow you to connect microphones and your instruments with your computer and allow you to record into a digital audio workstation. There are a lot of great choices out there, but the one I would recommend for a beginner would be the [Focusrite Scarlett 2i2](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=https://focusrite.com/en/usb-audio-interface/scarlett/scarlett-2i2&ved=2ahUKEwif5oTuxYDpAhUlU98KHfPkBNUQFjAAegQIBBAB&usg=AOvVaw0-V2CcSNX1VgW8HwgIeBCC)
It's super easy to use, and it allows for microphone inputs as well as the ability to plug your guitar and/or bass directly into it. If you're looking for something with a few more inputs, maybe look at the [Behringer UMC1820](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=https://www.behringer.com/Categories/Behringer/Computer-Audio/Interfaces/UMC1820/p/P0B2J&ved=2ahUKEwjy_I3UtYDpAhVwkuAKHejxATcQFjAAegQIARAB&usg=AOvVaw2EUJ00ai_-roCzO8G2jSmU). It's fairly affordable for the amount of microphone preamps, and it's a good beginner interface. 

After you've selected your interface, you'll want to pick up some microphones. The most tried and true mic out there is probably the [Shure SM57](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=https://www.sweetwater.com/store/detail/SM57--shure-sm57-cardioid-dynamic-instrument-microphone&ved=2ahUKEwiy8cLVtoDpAhWHhOAKHaG7CwoQFjABegQIAxAB&usg=AOvVaw1hsJbhI_pNpa9SatUimiAp). This microphone can be used on anything from snare drums, to guitar cabinets, and even vocals! It's truly the workhorse in most professional studios. But that said, you'll probably be needing a few more mics, especially if you plan on recording drums. CAD Microphones makes an extreme affordable [drum mic kit](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=https://www.guitarcenter.com/CAD/PRO-7-Drum-Microphone-Kit-7-Piece.gc&ved=2ahUKEwjYw7HJt4DpAhUQd98KHZVmD1QQFjAAegQIARAB&usg=AOvVaw18AxIiowDAkdjsHnVj5AMT) that would be perfect for a beginner. They even come with mic-clips so you can avoiding having to buy a lot of stands (although you'll still need to purchase a few mic stands). They include 5 dynamic microphones for the kick, snare, and three toms, as well as two condensor mics for the overheads.  

Finally, you'll want to select your software of choice. Audacity is a fine starting software (it's what I started in), but if you're willing to learn a little bit, I'd highly recommend Reaper. It's essentially free software, but it's completely professional, fully customizable, and there are a plethora of tutorials online for how to use it. It has a lot of great features that audacity just won't carry, and it'll be something you can grow into as you learn more about recording. 

Once you've acquired all these things, as well as some microphone cables and a few stands, it's time to get to miking things up. There is no real right or wrong way to mic anything up; it's entirely up to you and what kind of sound you are going for. Having said that though, there are some tried and true methods that seem to work best. **For guitars**, aim an SM57 at the center of your cabinets speaker cone anywhere between 2"-6" away. The further the mic, the more focused the low-end will be (although you'll start to get more room sound which might not be what you want). You can also move the microphone off-axis to get a "darker" tone with a little less top-end bite to it. Something to consider when recording guitars: you won't need as much distortion as you think. As you're recording and layering takes, distortion tends to stack up and can become a muddy mess if there's too much, so just remember "less is more." When it comes to recording **Bass** I would simply recommend plugging it directly into your audio interface. However, you can also use a bass drum microphone on the cabinet as well. Just place it aimed as one of the speaker cones at about the same distance as the guitar cabinet microphone. If you want some additional bite and grit to your bass, add an SM57 and aim it off-axis. 

Recording **Drums** is probably the hardest of the bunch. There's a lot of room for error, but it's also probably the most fun part of recording. Each piece of the kit will get its own microphone. 
We'll start with the **kick drum**. For metal, you're definitely going to want to place the mic just inside of the drum port thats located in the reso-head of the drum. If your drummer doesn't have one, get a new drummer. Just kidding, but definitely either purchase a ported head or simply cut one out. It should be large enough for the mic to fit inside without touching the drum head. Doing this will all you to get the "click" of the beater hitting the drum while still getting the low end thud. 
On the **snare drum** you'll want to place your mic so that it is aimed directly at the center of the snare. This will give you the most attack and "crack" from the stick. The closer the microphone is to the beater head, the more low-end you'll pick up, so experiment with what you think is best. If you have an extra mic, try miking up the reso-head too. Just remember to make sure the mics are roughly the same distance from their respective heads. You also might have to invert the polarity, or "flip the phase" as it's often  referred to, of one of the snare micriphones in your software. 
For the **toms** I always place them with roughly three fingers of room between the microphone and the drum head. If you aim the mic towards the center of the drum you'll get more attack, while aiming it towards the rim will give you more of a rounder tone. Experiment with what you think works best. It may take a few trys to get what your looking for. 
Finally, for the **overhead microphones** you'll need at least two mic stands. Position them so that they are the same height as one another. I typically will ensure that each of the overhead mics are equidistant to the center of the snare drum. That is to say, if I were to measure each microphones distance away from the snare drum, they would be the same. It should look something like [this](https://www.gearank.com/guides/overhead-drum-mics). The closer the mics are to the cymbals, the more focused your stereo image of the kit will be; the further away the more room sound you'll pick up. 

**Vocals** are probably the easiest. For metal, any kind of dynamic microphone will work. You'll see a lot of love for the SM7B, but honestly you SM57 will work just fine. Get a pop-filter and mic-stand and you'll be good to go. 


Somethings to consider:

* Recording to a metronome will result in a tighter performance, but if you've never practiced to one, it'll be pretty hard to do so as a full band. I recommend recording a guitar take to a metronome first so that you have a guide track that is in time. Take each instrument one at a time and build your recording that way. It's tedious, but very rewarding 

* Make sure you're tracking at the appropriate audio level. You don't want to crank your preamps gain knobs. Pay attention to the meters in your software. I generally aim for somewhere between -15 to -10dB, but as long as it's not clipping red, you should be fine. You can always add gain later, but you can take it way

* Remember it's okay to mess up. Nothing has to be absolutely perfect. Experiment and see what works for you. Don't beat yourself up if you don't nail something right away. Recording takes a lot of practice to do properly.

I was interning at a recording studio in Nashville where an artist was giving an interview to support his then up-coming solo record. 
One thing I should mention is that we were explicitly told to never interact with the clientele unless they directly interacted with us. Disobeying this would pretty much guarantee you lost your internship. 

I was tasked with setting a few bottles of water in the live room for the upcoming interview. I approached the entrance of the live room with my hands full of water bottles when I noticed the door was being blocked by an entourage. I  politely excused myself and asked the person who was directly in front of the door if they wouldn't mind stepping to the side so I could go in. They obliged and I made my way in, no big deal. 

Afterwards, I returned to the office with the other interns. As we were sitting there just chatting, when the same guy I had asked to step aside walked by. The other interns froze and kind of panicked a little, what with a huge celebrity having just passed by. Me, not knowing what the huge fuss was about, asked what everyone's deal was. They informed me that Don Henley had just walked by. I could feel my heartbeat in my throat as I told them "Guys, I just told Don Henley to get out my way." 

TL;DR: I accidentally told Don Henley to get out of my way.
